title: Javascript Alerts - Adding Behaviour to Websites
summary: First hands-on JavaScript: running alert() in Chrome's DevTools console and Snippets editor, reading a ReferenceError, looking things up on MDN, and learning the grammar (function name, parentheses, string quotes, semicolon) plus style conventions.

concepts.heading: Two places to run JavaScript in Chrome
points: DevTools Console (View > Developer > JavaScript Console, or Cmd+Option+J / Ctrl+Shift+J): executes each line the moment Enter is pressed. Good for testing one-liners.
In the console, Shift+Enter inserts a new line without running, needed for multi-line input. Forgetting it and pressing Enter loses the half-written code.

Sources tab > left-hand panel arrow > Snippets: create a snippet (+ New snippet, e.g. index.js), write many lines, then run the whole file with the run button at the bottom right (or Cmd/Ctrl+Enter). This works like a mini editor and is what the next lessons use for exercises.
Output from the run appears in the console; each statement runs in order, and a dialog must be dismissed before the next line executes.

concepts.heading: The alert function
points: alert("Hello"); shows a pop-up with that message and an OK button. It is a function: a built-in piece of behaviour the browser knows how to perform.
Anatomy: the function name (alert), parentheses holding the argument (the message), quotation marks marking text as a string rather than code, and a semicolon ending the instruction.
alert is a method of the global window object, so window.alert("Hello"); is the long form. The short form is standard practice.
The message can be any text; the browser does not interpret it.

concepts.heading: Errors and finding valid keywords
points: Calling an unknown name, such as say("Hello"), stops the script with Uncaught ReferenceError: say is not defined. It means the browser has no function or variable with that name.
Code before the faulty line still ran; execution halts at the error.
MDN Web Docs (JavaScript section) is the reference for valid keywords and syntax. Searching 'alert' leads to Window.alert(), which shows the syntax, an example and the result.

concepts.heading: Syntax is grammar
points: Semicolon is like a full stop: it ends one instruction so the browser does not merge it with the next line.
Quotes mark a string; the contents are text, not code.
Parentheses hold what the function should receive.
Different languages (Ruby, Python, Java) use different symbols for the same ideas.

concepts.heading: Style conventions
points: Use straight code quotes, never typographic 'curly' quotes. Word processors and note apps substitute curly ones, which break code when pasted. Code editors insert the correct ones.
No spaces between the function name, parentheses, quotes and semicolon: alert("Hello");. Extra spaces work but are not the convention.
Single or double quotes behave identically for strings; the common convention for text is double quotes. (She notes single quotes are preferred in some situations later.)
A JavaScript style guide (she points to a community-maintained one) states the goal: code should look as though one person wrote it. Bookmark one and revisit it as you gain experience.

pitfalls: Pasting code from Word, Notes or web pages that contain curly quotes.
Pressing Enter instead of Shift+Enter when writing multi-line code in the console.
Misspelling a built-in name (Alert vs alert); JavaScript is case-sensitive.
Leaving out the closing quote or parenthesis.
